o: We may double elements up to k times total (k ≤ 15) to maximize the OR of the array. Doubling shifts bits left, creating fresh high bits. Key observation: applying all k doublings to a single element is optimal-ish because spreading doublings across elements creates overlapping low bits, whereas concentrating them reaches higher bit positions. Since k ≤ 15 and n can be large, we precompute prefix OR and suffix OR arrays; then for each element i and each split t (give i t doublings, others get none), candidate = (nums[i] << t) | prefixOR(i−1) | suffixOR(i+1). Take the max. Example: [8,1,2], k=2 → 8<<2=32, 32|1|2=35.
k: All k doublings go to one element; enumerate which one and how many (0..k).
Prefix/suffix OR arrays let each candidate be evaluated in O(1).

a.i: If element i receives t doublings, the rest of the array is unchanged, contributing prefixOR[0..i−1] | suffixOR[i+1..]. Trying every (i, t) covers the optimal solution since concentrating doublings dominates splitting them (splitting only produces bits ≤ those achievable by concentration on the highest-value element).
s: Build pre[i] = OR of nums[0..i−1] and suf[i] = OR of nums[i+1..n−1].
For each i, for t in 0..k, candidate = (nums[i] << t) | pre[i] | suf[i+1].
a.t: O(nk) — prefix/suffix builds are O(n); the double loop is O(nk) with k ≤ 15

a.n: Approach 2: Bit-count trick (single pass over candidates)
a.i: Alternative formulation: compute total OR and, for each element, the OR of all other elements using counts of how many elements have each bit set (remove element i's contribution per bit). Equivalent complexity but avoids explicit prefix arrays.
s: Count, for each bit b, how many numbers have it; also compute total OR.
For each i, restOr = OR over bits where count[b] − (bit set in nums[i] ? 1 : 0) ≥ 1.
Try all t doublings of nums[i] against restOr.

w: In an interview, justify why all doublings go to one element: shifting one element t times reaches bit position higher than any combination of smaller shifts, and OR only adds bits. Pitfalls: 64-bit results (nums[i] << 15 exceeds int range) — use long/BigInt; JavaScript bitwise ops are 32-bit, hence BigInt there. Edge case: k applied to already-huge values; single-element arrays. Follow-up: what if operations were multiply-by-3 instead of doubling?
